claim: Response inhibition is essential for navigating everyday life.
source: Response inhibition is essential for navigating everyday life.
evidence: This is a general statement presented as established knowledge in the abstract without specific supporting data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Derailment of response inhibition is considered integral to numerous neurological and psychiatric disorders.
source: Its derailment is considered integral to numerous neurological and psychiatric disorders, and more generally, to a wide range of behavioral and health problems.
evidence: This statement reflects established scientific consensus in the field, as indicated by the phrase 'is considered'.

claim: Response-inhibition efficiency correlates with treatment outcome in some neurological and psychiatric conditions.
source: Response-inhibition efficiency furthermore correlates with treatment outcome in some of these conditions.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge without specific citations in this sentence.

claim: The stop-signal task is an essential tool to determine how quickly response inhibition is implemented.
source: The stop-signal task is an essential tool to determine how quickly response inhibition is implemented.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge about the purpose and utility of the stop-signal task.

claim: The stop-signal task was developed by Lappin and Eriksen (1966), Logan and Cowan (1984), and Vince (1948).
source: The stop-signal task (Lappin and Eriksen, 1966; Logan and Cowan, 1984; Vince, 1948) is an essential tool for studying response inhibition in neuroscience, psychiatry, and psychology (among several other disciplines; see Appendix 1), and is used across various human (e.g. clinical vs. non-clinical, different age groups) and non-human (primates, rodents, etc.) populations.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original publications that developed the task.

claim: The stop-signal task is used across various human and non-human populations.
source: The stop-signal task (Lappin and Eriksen, 1966; Logan and Cowan, 1984; Vince, 1948) is an essential tool for studying response inhibition in neuroscience, psychiatry, and psychology (among several other disciplines; see Appendix 1), and is used across various human (e.g. clinical vs. non-clinical, different age groups) and non-human (primates, rodents, etc.) populations.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the broad application of the task.

claim: In the stop-signal task, participants perform a go task but on a minority of trials a stop signal appears after a variable stop-signal delay instructing participants to suppress the imminent go response.
source: In this task, participants typically perform a go task (e.g. press left when an arrow pointing to the left appears, and right when an arrow pointing to the right appears), but on a minority of the trials, a stop signal (e.g. a cross replacing the arrow) appears after a variable stop-signal delay (SSD), instructing participants to suppress the imminent go response (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the basic structure of the task, with reference to Figure 1 for visual illustration.

claim: Response-inhibition latency cannot be observed directly because successful response inhibition results in the absence of an observable response.
source: Unlike the latency of go responses, response-inhibition latency cannot be observed directly (as successful response inhibition results in the absence of an observable response).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of successful inhibition.

claim: The stop-signal task is unique in allowing the estimation of covert response-inhibition latency (SSRT).
source: The stop-signal task is unique in allowing the estimation of this covert latency (stop-signal reaction time or SSRT; Box 1).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the unique capability of the task.

claim: Links exist between inhibitory-control capacities and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.
source: Research using the task has revealed links between inhibitory-control capacities and a wide range of behavioral and impulse-control problems in everyday life, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, substance abuse, eating disorders, and obsessive-compulsive behaviors (for meta-analyses, see e.g. Bartholdy et al., 2016; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analytic reviews.

claim: Links exist between inhibitory-control capacities and substance abuse.
source: Research using the task has revealed links between inhibitory-control capacities and a wide range of behavioral and impulse-control problems in everyday life, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, substance abuse, eating disorders, and obsessive-compulsive behaviors (for meta-analyses, see e.g. Bartholdy et al., 2016; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analytic reviews.

claim: Links exist between inhibitory-control capacities and eating disorders.
source: Research using the task has revealed links between inhibitory-control capacities and a wide range of behavioral and impulse-control problems in everyday life, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, substance abuse, eating disorders, and obsessive-compulsive behaviors (for meta-analyses, see e.g. Bartholdy et al., 2016; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analytic reviews.

claim: Links exist between inhibitory-control capacities and obsessive-compulsive behaviors.
source: Research using the task has revealed links between inhibitory-control capacities and a wide range of behavioral and impulse-control problems in everyday life, including attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, substance abuse, eating disorders, and obsessive-compulsive behaviors (for meta-analyses, see e.g. Bartholdy et al., 2016; Lipszyc and Schachar, 2010; Smith et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to meta-analytic reviews.

claim: There is considerable heterogeneity in how stop-signal studies are designed and executed.
source: Currently, there is considerable heterogeneity in how stop-signal studies are designed and executed, how the SSRT is estimated, and how results of stop-signal studies are reported.
evidence: This is an observation about the current state of the field, likely based on the authors' collective knowledge and review of the literature.

claim: Small design details can have an immense impact on the nature of the stop process and the task.
source: First, what might seem like small design details can have an immense impact on the nature of the stop process and the task.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge based on the authors' expertise.

claim: SSRT estimates are unreliable when inappropriate estimation methods are used or when the underlying race-model assumptions are seriously violated.
source: Second, SSRT estimates are unreliable when inappropriate estimation methods are used or when the underlying race-model assumptions are (seriously) violated (see Box 1 for a discussion of the race model).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the conditions that affect SSRT reliability.

claim: The validity of SSRT can be checked only if researchers report all relevant methodological information and data.
source: Third, the validity of SSRT can be checked only if researchers report all relevant methodological information and data.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for validating SSRT estimates.

claim: The authors agreed on 12 recommendations that should safeguard and improve the quality of future stop-signal research.
source: After an extensive consultation round, the authors of the present paper agreed on 12 recommendations that should safeguard and further improve the overall quality of future stop-signal research.
evidence: This describes the consensus process and outcome of the current manuscript.

claim: The recommendations are based on previous methodological studies or novel simulations.
source: The recommendations are based on previous methodological studies or, where further empirical support was required, on novel simulations (which are reported in Appendices 2–3).
evidence: This describes the basis for the recommendations, including both existing literature and new simulations conducted for this study.

claim: Standard two-choice reaction time tasks are recommended for most purposes and populations.
source: Standard two-choice reaction time tasks (e.g. in which participants have to discriminate between left and right arrows) are recommended for most purposes and populations.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: When very simple go tasks are used, the go stimulus and the stop signal will closely overlap in time, leading to violations of the race model.
source: When very simple go tasks are used, the go stimulus and the stop signal will closely overlap in time (because the SSD has to be very short to still allow for the possibility to inhibit a response), leading to violations of the race model as stop-signal presentation might interfere with encoding of the go stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of the task and the race model assumptions.

claim: Substantially increasing the difficulty of the go task might influence the stop process.
source: Substantially increasing the difficulty of the go task (e.g. by making the discrimination much harder) might also influence the stop process (e.g. the underlying latency distribution or the probability that the stop process is triggered).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential effects of task difficulty, indicated by the word 'might'.

claim: Very simple and very difficult go tasks should be avoided unless the researcher has theoretical or methodological reasons for using them.
source: Thus, very simple and very difficult go tasks should be avoided unless the researcher has theoretical or methodological reasons for using them (for example, simple detection tasks have been used in animal studies. To avoid responses before the go stimulus is presented or close overlap between the presentation of go stimulus and stop signal, the intertrial interval can be drawn from a random exponential distribution. This will make the occurrence of the go stimulus unpredictable, discouraging anticipatory responses).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: The 'anticipatory response' variant of the stop-signal task holds promise.
source: While two-choice tasks are the most common, we note that the 'anticipatory response' variant of the stop-signal task (in which participants have to press a key when a moving indicator reaches a stationary target) also holds promise (e.g. Leunissen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study demonstrating this variant.

claim: SSRT is the overall latency of a chain of processes involved in stopping a response, including the detection of the stop signal.
source: SSRT is the overall latency of a chain of processes involved in stopping a response, including the detection of the stop signal.
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge about what SSRT represents.

claim: Salient, easily detectable stop signals should be used unless researchers are specifically interested in perceptual or attentional processes.
source: Unless researchers are specifically interested in such perceptual or attentional processes, salient, easily detectable stop signals should be used (when auditory stop signals are used, these should not be too loud either, as very loud (i.e. >80 dB) auditory stimuli may produce a startle reflex).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: Very loud auditory stimuli (>80 dB) may produce a startle reflex.
source: Unless researchers are specifically interested in such perceptual or attentional processes, salient, easily detectable stop signals should be used (when auditory stop signals are used, these should not be too loud either, as very loud (i.e. >80 dB) auditory stimuli may produce a startle reflex).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the effects of loud auditory stimuli.

claim: Salient stop signals will reduce the relative contribution of perceptual (afferent) processes to the SSRT.
source: Salient stop signals will reduce the relative contribution of perceptual (afferent) processes to the SSRT, and the probability that within- or between-group differences can be attributed to them.
evidence: This is an inference about the effects of using salient stop signals.

claim: Salient stop signals might reduce the probability of 'trigger failures' on stop trials.
source: Salient stop signals might also reduce the probability of a 'trigger failures' on stop trials (see Box 2).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential effects, indicated by the word 'might'.

claim: When participants strategically wait for a stop signal to occur, the nature of the stop-signal process and task change.
source: When participants strategically wait for a stop signal to occur, the nature of the stop-signal process and task change (complicating the comparison between conditions or groups; e.g. SSRT group differences might be caused by differential slowing or strategic adjustments).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the effects of waiting strategies.

claim: SSRT estimates will become less reliable when participants wait for the stop signal to occur.
source: Importantly, SSRT estimates will also become less reliable when participants wait for the stop signal to occur (Verbruggen et al., 2013, see also Figure 2 and Appendix 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and reference to data presented in Figure 2 and Appendix 2.

claim: For standard stop-signal studies, 25% stop signals is recommended.
source: For standard stop-signal studies, 25% stop signals is recommended.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: If participants can predict when a stop signal will occur within a trial, they might wait for it.
source: If participants can predict when a stop signal will occur within a trial, they might also wait for it.
evidence: This is an inference about participant behavior based on predictability.

claim: A broad range of SSDs is required to prevent participants from predicting when a stop signal will occur.
source: Therefore, a broad range of SSDs is required.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on inference about preventing predictability.

claim: The stop-signal delay can be continuously adjusted via a standard adaptive tracking procedure that converges on a probability of responding of approximately 0.50.
source: The stop-signal delay can be continuously adjusted via a standard adaptive tracking procedure: SSD increases after each successful stop, and decreases after each unsuccessful stop; this converges on a probability of responding [p(respond|signal)] ≈ 0.50.
evidence: This describes the standard tracking procedure and its properties, which is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Many studies adjust SSD in steps of 50 ms.
source: Many studies adjust SSD in steps of 50 ms (which corresponds to three screen 'refreshes' for 60 Hz monitors).
evidence: This is an observation about common practice in the field.

claim: When step size is too small (for example 16 ms) the tracking may not converge in short experiments.
source: When step size is too small (for example 16 ms) the tracking may not converge in short experiments, whereas it may not be sensitive enough if step size is too large.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the effects of step size on tracking convergence.

claim: SSD should decrease after all responses on unsuccessful stop trials, including premature responses and choice errors.
source: Importantly, SSD should decrease after all responses on unsuccessful stop trials; this includes premature responses on unsuccessful stop trials (i.e. responses executed before the stop signal was presented) and choice errors on unsuccessful stop trials (e.g. when a left go response would have been executed on the stop trial depicted in Figure 1, even though the arrow was pointing to the right).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise, with reference to Figure 1 for illustration.

claim: An adaptive tracking procedure typically results in a sufficiently varied set of SSD values.
source: An adaptive tracking procedure typically results in a sufficiently varied set of SSD values.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the properties of the tracking procedure.

claim: The tracking procedure requires fewer stop trials to obtain a reliable SSRT estimate.
source: An additional advantage of the tracking procedure is that fewer stop trials are required to obtain a reliable SSRT estimate (Band et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a methodological study.

claim: The tracking procedure is recommended for standard applications.
source: Thus, the tracking procedure is recommended for standard applications.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: Task instructions should be used to discourage waiting in human studies.
source: In human studies, task instructions should also be used to discourage waiting.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: Participants should be told to respond as quickly as possible to the go stimulus and not wait for the stop signal to occur.
source: At the very least, participants should be told that '[they] should respond as quickly as possible to the go stimulus and not wait for the stop signal to occur' (or something along these lines).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: The tracking procedure can be explained to adults to further discourage a waiting strategy.
source: To adults, the tracking procedure (if used) can also be explained to further discourage a waiting strategy (i.e. inform participants that the probability of an unsuccessful stop trial will approximate 0.50, and that SSD will increase if they gradually slow their responses).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: Inclusion of a practice block in which adherence to instructions is carefully monitored is recommended.
source: Inclusion of a practice block in which adherence to instructions is carefully monitored is recommended.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: In certain populations, such as young children, it might be advisable to start with a practice block without stop signals to emphasize the importance of the go component of the task.
source: In certain populations, such as young children, it might furthermore be advisable to start with a practice block without stop signals to emphasize the importance of the go component of the task.
evidence: This is a speculative recommendation for specific populations, indicated by 'might be advisable'.

claim: Between blocks, participants should be reminded about the instructions and provided with block-based feedback.
source: Between blocks, participants should also be reminded about the instructions. Ideally, this is combined with block-based feedback, informing participants about their mean RT on go trials, number of go omissions (with a reminder that this should be 0), and p(respond|signal) (with a reminder that this should be close to .50).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: The number of stop trials varies widely between studies.
source: The number of stop trials varies widely between studies.
evidence: This is an observation about current practice in the field.

claim: Reliable and unbiased SSRT group-level estimates can be obtained with 50 stop trials, but only under optimal or very specific circumstances.
source: Our novel simulation results (see Figure 2 and Appendix 2) indicate that reliable and unbiased SSRT group-level estimates can be obtained with 50 stop trials (with 25% stop signals in an experiment, this amounts to 200 trials in total. Usually, this corresponds to an experiment of 7–10 min including breaks), but only under 'optimal' or very specific circumstances (e.g. when the probability of go omissions is low and the go-RT distribution is not strongly skewed).
evidence: This claim is based on novel simulation data presented in Figure 2 and Appendix 2.

claim: Lower trial numbers (25 stop trials) rarely produced reliable SSRT estimates.
source: Lower trial numbers (here we tested 25 stop trials) rarely produced reliable SSRT estimates (and the number of excluded subjects was much higher; see Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is based on simulation data presented in Figure 2.

claim: At least 50 stop trials are recommended for standard group-level comparisons.
source: Thus, as a general rule of thumb, we recommend to have at least 50 stop trials for standard group-level comparisons.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the simulation results.

claim: 50 stop trials may not suffice to obtain reliable individual estimates required for individual-differences research or diagnostic purposes.
source: However, it should again be stressed that this may not suffice to obtain reliable individual estimates (which are required for e.g. individual-differences research or diagnostic purposes).
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results and understanding of reliability requirements.

claim: Reliability of SSRT estimates increases with number of trials.
source: Thus, our simulations reported in Appendix 2 suggest that reliability increases with number of trials.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation data reported in Appendix 2.

claim: In some clinical populations, adding trials may not always be possible or might be counterproductive.
source: However, in some clinical populations, adding trials may not always be possible (e.g. when patients cannot concentrate for a sufficiently long period of time), and might even be counterproductive (as strong fluctuations over time can induce extra noise).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about practical limitations in clinical populations.

claim: For standard group-level comparisons, researchers can compensate for lower trial numbers by increasing sample size.
source: Our simulations reported in Appendix 3 show that for standard group-level comparisons, researchers can compensate for lower trial numbers by increasing sample size.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation data reported in Appendix 3.

claim: SSRTs can be estimated based on the independent race model, which assumes an independent race between a go and a stop runner.
source: SSRTs can be estimated based on the independent race model, which assumes an independent race between a go and a stop runner (Box 1).
evidence: This describes the theoretical foundation for SSRT estimation, which is established knowledge.

claim: When the independence assumption of the race model is seriously violated, SSRT estimates become unreliable.
source: When this independence assumption is (seriously) violated, SSRT estimates become unreliable (Band et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a methodological study.

claim: The independence assumption should be checked by comparing the mean RT on unsuccessful stop trials with the mean RT on go trials.
source: Therefore, the assumption should be checked. This can be done by comparing the mean RT on unsuccessful stop trials with the mean RT on go trials.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on established methodology.

claim: The comparison of RT on unsuccessful stop trials versus go trials should include all trials with a response and should be done for each participant and condition separately.
source: Note that this comparison should include all trials with a response (including choice errors and premature responses), and it should be done for each participant and condition separately.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: SSRT should not be estimated when RT on unsuccessful stop trials is numerically longer than RT on go trials.
source: SSRT should not be estimated when RT on unsuccessful stop trials is numerically longer than RT on go trials (see also, Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and supported by data in Appendix 2.

claim: A large number of stop trials is required for formal and in-depth tests of the race model to be meaningful and reliable.
source: More formal and in-depth tests of the race model can be performed (e.g. examining probability of responding and RT on unsuccessful stop trials as a function of delay); however, a large number of stop trials is required for such tests to be meaningful and reliable.
evidence: This is an inference based on statistical considerations for testing the race model.

claim: When the tracking procedure is used, the 'mean estimation' method is the most popular SSRT estimation method.
source: When the tracking procedure is used, the 'mean estimation' method is still the most popular (presumably because it is very easy to use).
evidence: This is an observation about current practice in the field.

claim: The mean method is strongly influenced by the right tail (skew) of the go RT distribution.
source: However, the mean method is strongly influenced by the right tail (skew) of the go RT distribution (see Appendix 2 for examples), as well as by go omissions (i.e. go trials on which no response is executed).
evidence: This claim is supported by examples in Appendix 2.

claim: The mean method is strongly influenced by go omissions.
source: However, the mean method is strongly influenced by the right tail (skew) of the go RT distribution (see Appendix 2 for examples), as well as by go omissions (i.e. go trials on which no response is executed).
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the properties of the mean method.

claim: The integration method (which replaces go omissions with the maximum RT) is generally less biased and more reliable than the mean method when combined with the tracking procedure.
source: The simulations reported in Appendix 2 and summarized in Figure 2 indicate that the integration method (which replaces go omissions with the maximum RT in order to compensate for the lacking response) is generally less biased and more reliable than the mean method when combined with the tracking procedure.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation data presented in Appendix 2 and Figure 2.

claim: The integration method does not assume that p(respond|signal) is exactly 0.50.
source: Unlike the mean method, the integration method also does not assume that p(respond|signal) is exactly 0.50 (an assumption that is often not met in empirical data).
evidence: This describes a property of the integration method, which is established knowledge.

claim: The use of the integration method (with replacement of go omissions) is recommended when non-parametric estimation methods are used.
source: Therefore, we recommend the use of the integration method (with replacement of go omissions) when non-parametric estimation methods are used.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the simulation results.

claim: Some parametric SSRT estimation methods are less biased than even the best non-parametric methods.
source: Please note that some parametric SSRT estimation methods are less biased than even the best non-parametric methods and avoid other problems that can beset them (see Box 2); however, they can be harder for less technically adept researchers to use, and they may require more trials (see Matzke et al., 2018, for a discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a methodological discussion.

claim: Parametric SSRT estimation methods can be harder for less technically adept researchers to use and may require more trials.
source: Please note that some parametric SSRT estimation methods are less biased than even the best non-parametric methods and avoid other problems that can beset them (see Box 2); however, they can be harder for less technically adept researchers to use, and they may require more trials (see Matzke et al., 2018, for a discussion).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a methodological discussion.

claim: The integration method (with replacement of go omissions) is not completely immune to deviations in p(respond|signal) and go omissions.
source: Even though the preferred integration method (with replacement of go omissions) is less influenced by deviations in p(respond|signal) and go omissions than other methods, it is not completely immune to them either (Figure 2 and Appendix 2).
evidence: This claim is based on simulation data presented in Figure 2 and Appendix 2.

claim: SSRT estimates are most reliable when probability of responding on a stop trial is relatively close to 0.50.
source: Previous work suggests that SSRT estimates are most reliable (Band et al., 2003) when probability of responding on a stop trial is relatively close to 0.50.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a methodological study.

claim: Researchers should refrain from estimating individual SSRTs when p(respond|signal) is lower than 0.25 or higher than 0.75.
source: Therefore, we recommend that researchers refrain from estimating individual SSRTs when p(respond|signal) is lower than 0.25 or higher than 0.75 (Congdon et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and supported by a citation.

claim: As the probability of a go omission increases, SSRT estimates become less reliable.
source: Reliability of the estimates is also influenced by go performance. As the probability of a go omission increases, SSRT estimates also become less reliable.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about factors affecting SSRT reliability.

claim: Figure 2 and the resources described in Appendix 3 can be used to determine an acceptable level of go omissions at a study level.
source: Figure 2 and the resources described in Appendix 3 can be used to determine an acceptable level of go omissions at a study level.
evidence: This describes the utility of the provided resources based on the simulation data.

claim: Researchers should decide on cut-offs or exclusion criteria before data collection has started.
source: Importantly, researchers should decide on these cut-offs or exclusion criteria before data collection has started.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on best practices in research methodology.

claim: Researchers should carefully describe the stimuli, materials, and procedures used in the study to allow proper evaluation and replication.
source: To allow proper evaluation and replication of the study findings, and to facilitate follow-up studies, researchers should carefully describe the stimuli, materials, and procedures used in the study, and provide a detailed overview of the performed analyses (including a precise description of how SSRT was estimated).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on best practices in research methodology.

claim: The number of participants for whom SSRT was not estimated should be clearly mentioned.
source: The number of participants for whom SSRT was not estimated should be clearly mentioned.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on best practices in research reporting.

claim: Dependent variables which are directly observed should be separately reported for the participants that are not included in the SSRT analyses.
source: Ideally, dependent variables which are directly observed (see Recommendation 12) are separately reported for the participants that are not included in the SSRT analyses.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on best practices in research reporting.

claim: Researchers should clearly mention any exclusion criteria and whether those were set a-priori.
source: Researchers should also clearly mention any other exclusion criteria (e.g. outliers based on distributional analyses, acceptable levels of go omissions, etc.), and whether those were set a-priori (analytic plans can be preregistered on a public repository, such as the Open Science Framework; Nosek et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on best practices in research methodology, with a citation to support preregistration.

claim: Researchers should report all relevant descriptive statistics required to evaluate the findings of their stop-signal study.
source: Researchers should report all relevant descriptive statistics that are required to evaluate the findings of their stop-signal study (see Box 3 for a check-list).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on best practices in research reporting.

claim: Researchers are encouraged to share their anonymized raw (single-trial) data when possible.
source: Finally, we encourage researchers to share their anonymized raw (single-trial) data when possible (in accordance with the FAIR data guidelines; Wilkinson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on best practices in open science, with a citation to the FAIR data guidelines.

claim: If properly used, the stop-signal task can reveal unique information about the underlying neuro-cognitive control mechanisms.
source: If properly used, the task can reveal unique information about the underlying neuro-cognitive control mechanisms.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the potential of the task.

claim: The paper aims to increase the quality of research in the response-inhibition and impulse-control domain and to accelerate its progress.
source: By providing clear recommendations, and open-source resources, this paper aims to further increase the quality of research in the response-inhibition and impulse-control domain and to significantly accelerate its progress across the various important domains in which it is routinely applied.
evidence: This describes the goal of the current manuscript.

claim: The independent race model provides two common 'non-parametric' methods for estimating SSRT: the integration method and the mean method.
source: The independent race model (Box 1) provides two common 'non-parametric' methods for estimating SSRT: the integration method and the mean method.
evidence: This describes established methods for SSRT estimation.

claim: In the integration method, the point at which the stop process finishes is estimated by 'integrating' the RT distribution and finding the point at which the integral equals p(respond|signal).
source: In the integration method, the point at which the stop process finishes (Box 1) is estimated by 'integrating' the RT distribution and finding the point at which the integral equals p(respond|signal).
evidence: This describes the procedure for the integration method, which is established methodology.

claim: When combined with the tracking procedure, overall p(respond|signal) is used in the integration method.
source: When combined with the tracking procedure, overall p(respond|signal) is used.
evidence: This describes a specific implementation detail of the integration method.

claim: To determine the nth RT in the integration method, all go trials with a response are included (including go trials with a choice error and go trials with a premature response).
source: To determine the nth RT, all go trials with a response are included (including go trials with a choice error and go trials with a premature response).
evidence: This describes a specific implementation detail of the integration method.

claim: In the integration method, go omissions are assigned the maximum RT in order to compensate for the lacking response.
source: Importantly, go omissions (i.e. go trials on which the participant did not respond before the response deadline) are assigned the maximum RT in order to compensate for the lacking response.
evidence: This describes a specific implementation detail of the integration method.

claim: Premature responses on unsuccessful stop trials should be included when calculating p(respond|signal) and mean SSD.
source: Premature responses on unsuccessful stop trials (i.e. responses executed before the stop signal is presented) should also be included when calculating p(respond|signal) and mean SSD (as noted in Recommendation 4, SSD should also be adjusted after such trials).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the authors' consensus and expertise.

claim: The integration method with replacement of go omissions produces the most reliable and least biased non-parametric SSRT estimates.
source: This version of the integration method produces the most reliable and least biased non-parametric SSRT estimates (Appendix 2).
evidence: This claim is based on simulation data presented in Appendix 2.

claim: The mean method uses the mean of the inhibition function, which describes the relationship between p(respond|signal) and SSD.
source: The mean method uses the mean of the inhibition function (which describes the relationship between p(respond|signal) and SSD).
evidence: This describes the procedure for the mean method, which is established methodology.

claim: The mean method assumes that the mean RT equals SSRT + mean SSD.
source: In other words, the mean method assumes that the mean RT equals SSRT + mean SSD, so SSRT can be estimated easily by subtracting mean SSD from mean RT on go trials when the tracking procedure is used.
evidence: This describes an assumption of the mean method, which is established methodology.

claim: The simple version of the mean method is biased and generally less reliable than the integration method with replacement of go omissions.
source: However, our simulations show that this simple version of the mean method is biased and generally less reliable than the integration method with replacement of go omissions.
evidence: This claim is based on simulation data.
